definitions.definition: When a quantum system's many possibilities suddenly become one definite outcome, like a spinning coin landing on heads.
definitions.example: A particle that could be anywhere is suddenly found in one spot when you measure it.

definitions.definition: An endless series of observers needed to measure a quantum system, where each observer must be measured by another, never stopping.
definitions.example: Like a line of people each looking at the person in front, but no one ever sees the first person.

definitions.definition: Rules for combining mathematical symbols that represent actions or measurements in quantum mechanics.
definitions.example: Like learning how to add and multiply numbers, but with special symbols that represent things like position or energy.

definitions.definition: A complete mathematical space where quantum states live, like an infinite-dimensional coordinate system.
definitions.example: Imagine a graph that goes on forever in every direction, where each point is a possible state of a quantum system.

definitions.definition: The smooth, predictable change of a quantum system over time, without any sudden jumps.
definitions.example: Like a ball rolling smoothly down a hill, not teleporting from top to bottom.

definitions.definition: An endless chain where each step depends on the previous one, never reaching a starting point.
definitions.example: Like saying 'I know because my teacher said so, and their teacher said so, and so on forever.'

definitions.definition: The puzzle of how a quantum system goes from many possibilities to one definite outcome when measured.
definitions.example: Like a coin that is both heads and tails until you look at it, then it's just one.

definitions.definition: The idea that quantum systems just collapse when measured, without explaining how or why.
definitions.example: Like saying 'the coin lands on heads because it does,' without explaining the physics.

definitions.definition: The idea that every quantum possibility actually happens, but in separate parallel universes.
definitions.example: Like every time you flip a coin, one universe gets heads and another gets tails.

definitions.definition: The idea that quantum possibilities seem to disappear because they get mixed up with the environment, not because they actually collapse.
definitions.example: Like ripples in a pond that spread out and become invisible, but are still there.

definitions.definition: When waves combine to make bigger or smaller waves, or cancel each other out.
definitions.example: Like two ripples in a pond meeting and making a bigger ripple or flattening out.

definitions.definition: Using the rules of operator algebra to analyze a problem.
definitions.example: Like solving a puzzle by only using the specific rules of a game.

definitions.definition: The study of what exists and what it means for something to be real.
definitions.example: Asking whether numbers are real things or just ideas in our heads.

definitions.definition: The study of how we know things and what counts as knowledge.
definitions.example: Asking whether you can trust your senses or if you need proof.

definitions.definition: A Greek word meaning 'word' or 'reason,' used in the Bible to describe Jesus as the principle of order in the universe.
definitions.example: Like the blueprint or logic that makes the universe work.

definitions.definition: A central equation in the Theophysics framework that describes how reality works, involving many variables.
definitions.example: Like a super-complicated recipe that explains everything from atoms to galaxies.

definitions.definition: The belief that consciousness is a basic part of reality, not something that comes from physical processes.
definitions.example: Like saying the mind is more basic than the brain, not the other way around.

definitions.definition: The belief that the most basic stuff of reality is information, not matter or energy.
definitions.example: Like saying the universe is made of bits and bytes, not atoms.

definitions.definition: When the order of operations matters, so A then B gives a different result than B then A.
definitions.example: Like putting on socks then shoes vs. shoes then socks — different results.

definitions.definition: A mathematical way to measure how much two operations depend on order, written as [A,B] = AB - BA.
definitions.example: Like checking if putting on socks then shoes is the same as shoes then socks.

definitions.definition: A meeting of Christian leaders in 325 AD that defined the core beliefs about Jesus and God.
definitions.example: Like a big conference where they wrote down the rules of the faith.

definitions.definition: The rule that erasing one bit of information always produces a tiny amount of heat, at least kT ln 2.
definitions.example: Like how your computer gets warm when it deletes files.

definitions.definition: A measure of how much a field spreads out from a point, like how much water flows out of a pipe.
definitions.example: Like measuring how much air comes out of a fan at different spots.

definitions.definition: The state of being without sin or moral flaw.
definitions.example: Like being perfectly good, never doing anything wrong.

definitions.definition: Having three parts or elements that work together.
definitions.example: Like a three-legged stool, where each leg is needed for stability.

definitions.definition: When different fields of study independently arrive at the same conclusion.
definitions.example: Like a biologist and a chemist both figuring out the same thing about DNA without talking to each other.

definitions.definition: A perfect one-to-one correspondence between two structures, showing they are essentially the same.
definitions.example: Like a map of a city that perfectly matches the actual streets, so you can use one to understand the other.

definitions.definition: The Christian belief about God as three persons (Father, Son, Holy Spirit) as defined by the Council of Nicaea.
definitions.example: Like the idea that God is one being but three distinct persons, like a family that is one unit.

definitions.definition: Three important Christian leaders from the 4th century who helped explain the Trinity.
definitions.example: Like famous teachers who wrote the textbook on how to understand God as three persons.

definitions.definition: A historical debate about whether the Holy Spirit comes from the Father alone or from both the Father and the Son.
definitions.example: Like arguing over whether a gift comes from one parent or both parents together.

definitions.definition: When a quantum system is in multiple states at the same time until measured.
definitions.example: Like a coin spinning in the air that is both heads and tails until it lands.

definitions.definition: When something refers to itself, like a sentence that talks about itself.
definitions.example: Like the sentence 'This sentence is false,' which creates a paradox.

definitions.definition: An operation that cannot be undone because information is lost.
definitions.example: Like erasing a whiteboard — you can't get the original writing back.

definitions.definition: The process of making something real or actual from a potential state.
definitions.example: Like turning a blueprint into a real building.

definitions.definition: A Greek word meaning 'same substance,' used in the Nicene Creed to say Jesus is fully God.
definitions.example: Like saying two coins are both made of the same metal, so they are the same kind of thing.

definitions.definition: An ancient Christian heresy that says God is one person who appears in three different forms or modes.
definitions.example: Like an actor playing three different roles, but being only one person.

definitions.definition: A way to combine two mathematical spaces into a larger one, like multiplying dimensions.
definitions.example: Like combining a line and a square to make a cube.

definitions.definition: A Latin word meaning 'and the Son,' added to the Nicene Creed to say the Holy Spirit comes from both the Father and the Son.
definitions.example: Like adding 'and from the child' to a statement about where a gift comes from.

definitions.definition: A Greek word meaning 'sin,' literally 'missing the mark' or 'deviation.'
definitions.example: Like an archer shooting an arrow that misses the target.

definitions.definition: Relating to the nature of being or existence.
definitions.example: Like asking whether a chair is really real or just an idea.

definitions.definition: A Greek term meaning 'mutual indwelling,' describing how each person of the Trinity lives in the others.
definitions.example: Like three dancers moving together so perfectly that each is fully present in the others' movements.

definitions.definition: A mathematical result that guarantees a certain point stays the same after a transformation.
definitions.example: Like a point on a map that doesn't move when you rotate the map.

definitions.definition: A mathematical space that looks like flat Euclidean space when you zoom in close.
definitions.example: Like the surface of the Earth, which looks flat when you're on it but is actually curved.

definitions.definition: A rule in quantum mechanics that gives the probability of finding a particle in a particular state.
definitions.example: Like a formula that tells you how likely it is to get heads when you flip a quantum coin.

definitions.definition: A mathematical proof that the Born Rule is the only way to assign probabilities in quantum mechanics.
definitions.example: Like proving there's only one fair way to bet on a quantum coin flip.

definitions.definition: The absolute value or magnitude of a number, ignoring its sign.
definitions.example: Like the distance from zero, so both 5 and -5 have a modulus of 5.

definitions.definition: The observable physical characteristics of an organism, like its appearance and behavior.
definitions.example: Like your eye color or height, which come from your genes and environment.

definitions.definition: A theoretical field that guides the development of an organism's shape and structure.
definitions.example: Like an invisible blueprint that tells cells how to form a hand or a foot.

definitions.definition: The study of signs and symbols and how they create meaning.
definitions.example: Like studying how a red light means 'stop' and a smile means 'happy.'

definitions.definition: The subjective, felt qualities of experiences, like the redness of red or the pain of a headache.
definitions.example: Like the difference between knowing what a strawberry tastes like and actually tasting it.

definitions.definition: The process of becoming holy or more like God, often associated with the Holy Spirit.
definitions.example: Like a gradual cleaning and improvement of a person's character.

definitions.definition: The Christian belief that Jesus's death repaired the broken relationship between humans and God.
definitions.example: Like saying sorry and making up for a mistake to restore a friendship.

definitions.definition: When quantum effects spread and get lost very quickly, like a chain reaction that grows exponentially.
definitions.example: Like a rumor that spreads and gets distorted faster and faster until no one knows the truth.

definitions.definition: The smallest possible scale of length, time, and energy where quantum gravity becomes important.
definitions.example: Like the ultimate zoom level where our usual ideas of space and time break down.

definitions.definition: Proven to be false by evidence or logical argument.
definitions.example: Like a theory that is shown to be wrong by an experiment.

definitions.definition: A type of operator in math that is equal to its own transpose, important in quantum mechanics for representing measurable quantities.
definitions.example: Like a mirror that reflects an image perfectly back to itself.

definitions.definition: A Hilbert space that has a countable basis, meaning it can be described by a list of basic states.
definitions.example: Like a library with a list of all the books, even if there are infinitely many.

definitions.definition: A fundamental field in the Theophysics framework that represents the coherence or order of reality.
definitions.example: Like a field of order that keeps the universe from falling into chaos.

definitions.definition: When waves or systems are in sync, maintaining a consistent relationship.
definitions.example: Like a choir singing in perfect harmony, not off-key.

definitions.definition: A concept in the Theophysics framework relating moral choices to the geometry of reality.
definitions.example: Like how a wrong choice might 'bend' the fabric of reality in a negative way.

definitions.definition: Based on observation or experience, not just theory.
definitions.example: Like a scientist doing an experiment and recording what happens.

definitions.definition: Able to be proven false by evidence, a key feature of scientific theories.
definitions.example: Like the claim 'all swans are white' can be proven false by finding one black swan.

definitions.definition: A basic statement that is assumed to be true without proof, used as a starting point for reasoning.
definitions.example: Like 'all right angles are equal' in geometry, which is accepted without proof.

definitions.definition: A statement that has been proven to be true using logic and axioms.
definitions.example: Like the Pythagorean theorem, which is proven from basic geometry rules.

definitions.definition: The study of salvation, how humans are saved from sin and its consequences.
definitions.example: Like studying how a person can be rescued from a dangerous situation.

definitions.definition: The study of sin, its origin, and its effects.
definitions.example: Like studying what 'missing the mark' means and how it affects people.

definitions.definition: A natural vibration pattern of a system, where all parts move together at a specific frequency.
definitions.example: Like the way a guitar string vibrates in a specific pattern when plucked.

definitions.definition: A function that summarizes the dynamics of a system, used to derive equations of motion.
definitions.example: Like a recipe that tells you how a ball will move when thrown.

definitions.definition: A one-to-one matching between two sets where every element in one set is paired with exactly one in the other, and vice versa.
